newsitem.title: BELARUS: Rival Belarus parliaments fight war of words.
newsitem.headline: Rival Belarus parliaments fight war of words.

text.p: Rival parliaments, one supporting hardline President Alexander Lukashenko and one opposing him, waged a war of words in Belarus on Tuesday as the president pressed home his victory in a referendum on Sunday.
Loyal supporters of Lukashenko, voting by raising their hands in Soviet-style unanimity, formalised the deep division in parliament over Lukashenko's rule by setting up their own breakaway assembly.
One pro-Lukashenko deputy, Ivan Pashkevich, told Reuters the rump of the old parliament, which tried unsuccessfully last week to impeach the president, would be left "on the rubbish-heap of history".

The numbers and the political momentum appeared to be in Lukashenko's favour after his crushing victory in the referendum, which critics said was a farce and which drew a statement of concern on Tuesday from the European Union.

Of the 199 members of the old parliament, 112 met behind closed doors in a building near the presidency and Lukashenko told them they would become the "House of Representatives," the lower chamber of his new parliament.

Their meeting was chaired by Yuri Malumov, a deputy speaker and the most senior parliamentary official to cross to Lukashenko's side. They voted unanimously to make the results of Sunday's voting binding and to halt a bid by the old parliament to impeach Lukashenko.

Members opposed to the president continued to sit in the main parliament building, but were unable to muster a quorum. "Let's stay honest to the end. Let's not go begging on our knees for crumbs at the president's table," one deputy, Ivan Shulakovsky, told 66 deputies at an afternoon session.
"We have the strongest force there is -- the moral right is on our side," speaker Semyon Sharetsky told them.
"Let him (Lukashenko) do what he wants. You should never pay attention to people who fly into rages and completely disregard the law," Sharetsky told Reuters in an interview in his office.
"We follow the power of laws. But there, they follow the law of power," he added.
"What referendum? It was a rape of the people," Sharetsky retorted when asked for his evaluation of the vote.
Lukashenko claimed that 70.5 percent of the electorate backed him in the plebiscite, giving him a mandate to proceed directly with reshaping the country's institutions.
Lukashenko promised that all the former deputies, including those who did not get seats in the new 110-member lower house, would retain their status and perks as members of parliament.
He was in magnanimous mood on Tuesday, saying the losers in his country's political crisis should not be punished.
Lukashenko's new legislature will also have an upper house or Senate, some of whose members he will appoint directly.

Vasily Baranov, an official of the Belarussian security council, told a news briefing that Russian Defence Minister Igor Rodionov would attend a ceremony on Wednesday to mark the withdrawal this month of the last nuclear missiles from Belarus.

Lukashenko confirmed that despite international criticism of his plebiscite he would be attending the summit next week of the Organisation for European Security and Cooperation in Europe in Lisbon. The OSCE was among organisations which refused to send observers to validate the poll.
The United States said Lukashenko's victory was "deprived of legitimacy" and the European Union said it was still seriously concerned about events in Belarus.
"The European Union remains seriously concerned at the situation in Belarus, and particularly the issue of the constitutional referendum," it said.

Lukashenko has paid little regard to Western criticism and his main ally Russia signalled on Tuesday it was unlikely to interfere with his plans providing he manages to resolve the situation without violence.
Russia briefly intervened last week to broker a short-lived compromise between Lukashenko and his foes but the deal collapsed within hours, leaving the president a free hand.
President Boris Yeltsin's spokesman told journalists in Moscow on Tuesday the president expected all those involved to display restraint and preserve civil peace.
"President Boris Yeltsin considers civic accord and prevention of violence an absolute priority," Yeltsin's press secretary Sergei Yastrzhembsky told a Kremlin briefing.
"He expects both sides to show restraint and adopt a balanced approach, believing that this is a key condition for a success in Russian-Belarussian integration."
Russia and Belarus agreed to unite in a "community" last April but Moscow has strong doubts about Lukashenko's autocratic style and lack of free-market economic reforms.
